title: Marcia Chatelain at Harvard Book Store
description: Harvard Book Store welcomes Marcia Chatelain —Presidential Penn Compact Professor of Africana studies at the University of Pennsylvania and Pulitzer Prize-winning author of Franchise —for a discussion of her new book, How Bright the Path Grows: The Untold Story of the Women Who Made the March on Washington. She will be joined in conversation by Christian Hosam —Assistant Professor of Political Science and Faculty Affiliate of the Albright Institute at Wellesley College. About How Bright the Path Grows From the Pulitzer Prize-winning author of Franchise comes the little-known story of the pioneering Black women artists and activists who were seen, but barely heard, at the 1963 March on Washington. There is no shortage of footage immortalizing the men who spoke at the 1963 March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, when 250,000 Americans gathered beneath the Lincoln Memorial to call for an end to segregation. There were reverends and rabbis, activists and Rat-Pack icons—and of course the day’s headliner, whose prophetic dream of a post-Jim Crow world has forever defined the Civil Rights Movement. But there is no “class photo” of the Black women who helped organize the march, performed on its main stage, or were honored during its “Tribute to Negro Women Fighters for Freedom.” In How Bright the Path Grows , Marcia Chatelain weaves a gleaming group portrait of these singular women. Among this cohort were several household names: vaudeville icon Josephine Baker; civil rights activist Rosa Parks gospel legend Mahalia Jackson, and Daisy Bates, champion of the Little Rock Nine. But many were relative unknowns, including Eva Jessye, the choir director who designed the day’s musical program, and Anna Hedgeman, the coordinator who pushed in the eleventh hour for a tribute to Black women’s work. description: Special Live Event! It’s been ten years, and we can still remember the fresh podcast. The recording equipment had never been used. The movies had never been watched. The Bechdel Cast was called “The Show of Dreams”… and it was, it really was! Join hosts Jamie Loftus and Caitlin Durante for a LIVE SHOW celebrating their TEN YEAR ANNIVERSARY of hosting The Bechdel Cast! Caitlin and Jamie are taking a look at the past decade of (genius, brilliant, important) discussions about film, and pondering how releasing radical mp3s every week didn’t fix global misogyny! title: Walking Tour: Reading the Urban Landscape
description: This event is at capacity. Join us for a special gallery talk that includes a walking tour! Graduate student teacher Ryan Schmidt-Knapik will first discuss the exhibition On Location: Drawing the Outdoors in the galleries before leading a walking tour on campus, where you will learn how to interpret and appreciate nature in our urban landscape. We will focus on exploring how humans shape the ecology of urban landscapes and how plants in these ecosystems in turn shape our relationship with nature. Led by: Ryan Schmidt-Knapik, Graduate student teacher and Ph.D. candidate in the Department of Organismic and Evolutionary Biology, Harvard University On Location: Drawing the Outdoors features drawings by J. M. W. Turner, John Constable, Gustave Courbet, Edouard Manet, Berthe Morisot, Paul Cézanne, and Vincent van Gogh, among many others. The exhibition is on view from September 18, 2026 to January 17, 2027. Funding for the exhibition and related programming was provided by the Stanley H. Durwood Foundation Support Fund, the Stanley H. Durwood Foundation Support Fund for the Study of Dutch Drawing, the Melvin R. Seiden and Janine Luke Fund for Publications and Exhibitions, and the M. Victor Leventritt Lecture Series Endowment Fund. The catalogue was made possible by the Andrew W. Mellon Publication Funds. Additional project support was provided by the Almathea Charitable Foundation.

Each class explores themes such as boundaries, self-trust, rest, joy, transition, and community. There is no right way to move and nothing to achieve. You are always encouraged to listen to your body, move at your own pace, and make the practice your own. All bodies and all levels are welcome. Tap is an American dance form in which rhythms are audibly tapped out on the floor. It has origins in slavery and the percussive dances of West African Juba dance and Irish step dancing. It developed through minstrel shows and vaudeville in the late 19th century and emerged along with jazz in the 20th century into the art form we know today. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? Sela has been a tap teacher since 2000, taking over Maureen Cosgrove’s Boston Tap classes at the Dance Complex in 2014. She was a founding member of the Terpsichore Ensemble in Amherst, MA and taught tap classes in Amherst and Northampton, MA before moving to Boston. title: 2026 Fall Exhibitions Opening Reception
description: Join us for the opening reception to celebrate two new exhibitions at the List Center: Uri Aran: Look How Hard They Work and Hao Jingban: I Witness. The opening reception will follow an Artist Talk with exhibiting artist, Hao Jingban, from 5:30-6:30PM. Exhibiting artists and exhibition curators will be in attendance. Light refreshments and beverages from Momma's Grocery + Wine will be served. Uri Aran: Look How Hard They Work Uri Aran's work is at once deeply idiosyncratic and oddly familiar: to follow it is to tinker alongside the artist, to be let in on an invention, or perhaps a shorthand between friends. Aran’s first major institutional solo exhibition in the United States gathers a new body of work: annotated panels that hover between quick line drawing and painting, welded sculptures that pose like equations, bulbous forms worked by hand in plasticene and foam, and a mass of piled-up googly eyes—the most elementary form of affect and animation—tragicomically raised to the scale of an earthwork. Hao Jingban: I Witness Blending documentary sensibility with poetic construction, Hao Jingban makes moving-image installations that are emotionally precise, historically incisive, and formally experimental. Hao’s first major US museum solo gathers recent work centered on I Witness (2025), a three-channel installation that takes up the embodied residue of the COVID-19 pandemic: four participants move slowly through a well-lit apartment, their images punctuated by stories of loss—an older woman who sleeps alone and rises to clean her refrigerator, a group of young people pacing an open field.

description: In this class, you’ll explore earthy Egyptian, Turkish, and American style movements, dynamic combinations, and expressive choreography blending tradition and innovation. Drawing from decades of study with master teachers and over thirty years of performance experience, Johara offers expert guidance in a supportive, inspiring environment—honoring the depth of this ancient art while inviting each student to discover their own unique style within it. The more authentic name for this dance form is raqs sharqi (“dance of the East”), and its roots lie in the Middle and Near East, primarily in Egypt and Turkey. This dance form was introduced to the United States and Europe at the turn of the 20th century, but it was not widely performed or taught until the 1950s and 1960s, when the belly dance craze swept across the U.S. The American cabaret style of belly dance is rooted in the legacy passed down by notable American teachers and performers, who blended Middle Eastern influences with their own innovations and movement styles drawn from diverse dance backgrounds. title: Akbar Shahid Ahmed at Harvard Book Store
description: Harvard Book Store welcomes Akbar Shahid Ahmed —award-winning journalist and Diplomatic Correspondent at NOTUS —for a discussion of his new book, Crossing the Red Line: Biden, His Advisors, and Israel’s War in Gaza. He will be joined in conversation by Indira Lakshmanan —award-winning journalist and co-host of WBUR’s Here & Now. About Crossing the Red Line A powerful and authoritative account of how the Biden administration fueled atrocities in Gaza, from an award-winning foreign affairs journalist. Following Hamas’s horrific October 7 attack, Israel launched an offensive of staggering violence in Gaza, saying it targeted militants while regularly striking hospitals, schools, and homes. Critically acclaimed journalist Akbar Shahid Ahmed offers extensive reporting and chilling new details about how the Biden administration enabled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu—ignoring warnings from government experts and implicating Americans in thousands of apparent war crimes. Washington did little to free Israeli hostages or shield innocent Palestinians as protests grew nationwide and international human rights principles crumbled. Still, President Joe Biden denied he was giving Netanyahu a blank check. He set a “red line” over the town of Rafah, where more than 1 million Palestinians were sheltering, saying an assault there would risk Israel’s pipeline of American bombs. Yet after Netanyahu’s advance began, deepening Gaza’s humanitarian catastrophe, Biden’s team kept weapons flowing. In vivid prose and with unparalleled access to insiders, Ahmed depicts a White House that resisted a course correction as its failures became undeniable. He probes Biden’s inner circle: a paranoid and imperious group shaped by the War on Terror, whose choices fueled tens of thousands of avoidable deaths among Palestinians, Lebanese, and Israelis, torpedoed long-time standards for warfare, and created a more dangerous world for us all. There will also be the first full-band onelinedrawing shows in forever in September and October, celebrating the 30th anniversary of Far’s TIn Cans With Strings To You, the 25th anniversary of Thriller, and of course the new album. Jonah started onelinedrawing in 1998, just as his first band, post-hardcore / emo misfits Far, was breaking up. The first onelinedrawing releases were a cassette on POPROCKIT, a label started by Kevin Seconds (7 Seconds). Then came the Sketchy EPs, first self-released, then in various forms on various indie labels (Crank, Revelation, Corrupted Image). During that time, onelinedrawing pioneered sliding-scale pricing for downloads and merch, monthly crowdfunded patronage (eventually released as the Always New albums), and Unique Recordings. During that time, onelinedrawing toured with and/or released music with Rival Schools, The Juliana Theory, Coheed & Cambria, Dashboard Confessional, Murder By Death, The Weakerthans, Jimmy Eat World, and more. onelinedrawing’s most recent studio album is Tenderwild, on Iodine Records. Iodine also recently released Sketchbook, a collection of early onelinedrawing recordings 1999-2001. onelinedrawing also has two albums (VISITOR and THE VOLUNTEERS) still on Jade Tree / Epitaph. Over 30 years, several projects, dozens of albums, hundreds of songs, and thousands of shows, Jonah Matranga has influenced countless artists: Deftones, Frank Turner, Thursday, My Chemical Romance, Walter Schreifels, and Chris Carraba. Capoeira is an Afro-Brazilian art form developed in Brazil by enslaved Africans and their descendants, bringing together elements of martial arts, movement, music, and cultural expression. Our practice of Capoeira Contemporânea is deeply rooted in the traditions of Capoeira Regional developed by Mestre Bimba. description: Harvard Book Store welcomes Jim Emison —retired Tennessee trial attorney, co-founder of Tennesseans for Historical Justice, and a board member of the Tennessee Historical Society—for a discussion of his book, Murder on the Hatchie: The NAACP’s First Martyr. He will be joined in conversation by Cornell William Brooks —Hauser Professor of the Practice of Nonprofit Organizations and Professor of the Practice of Public Leadership and Social Justice at the Harvard Kennedy School. About Murder on the Hatchie A groundbreaking work of true crime and civil rights history, Murder on the Hatchie uncovers the 1940 lynching of NAACP leader Elbert Williams–America’s first martyr for Black voting rights–and the federal failures that buried the case for more than eighty years. The forgotten lynching that launched America’s fight for Black voting rights–and the federal cover-up that followed. Murder on the Hatchie uncovers one of the earliest and most consequential crimes in America’s long struggle for Black voting rights: the 1940 lynching of Elbert Williams in Brownsville, Tennessee. A founding member of the local NAACP, Williams was murdered for attempting to register Black voters, decades before the more famous murders of Emmett Till and Medgar Evers. Through rigorous research and gripping narrative, retired trial attorney Jim Emison reconstructs the events surrounding Williams’s lynching and the federal government’s failure to prosecute his killers. Drawing on FBI files, Department of Justice correspondence, and eyewitness accounts, Emison reconstructs how white officials conspired to silence a community, implicating local law enforcement, federal agents, and even national NAACP leadership. Emison repositions Brownsville as a pivotal site in civil rights history and exposes how voter suppression, racial terror, and government complicity shaped the American democracy we inherit today. description: After graduating from Northern Illinois University, keyboardist and composer Brian Simpson relocated to Los Angeles where he was soon playing alongside musicians Gerald Albright and Norman Brown and eventually on a world tour with Janet Jackson. It was his tenure with George that led to working with a variety of artists, from James Ingram and Anita Baker to Dave Koz and Wayman Tisdale. title: C’port Textile & Book Drive, Oct. 24
description: ANNUAL TEXTILE/BOOK/VIDEO GAME DRIVE Sponsored by Cambridgeport Neighborhood Association (CAN) Clean Your Shelves; Reduce Waste; Help Non-Profits 10am to 2pm, October 24, 2026, in Hastings Square (corner of Brookline & Chestnut) Keep things out of landfills! Get your stuff to people who need it! Support the! Meet your neighbors! Bring all your unwanted, old, beat-up, or shelf-hogging books (as well as video games, DVDs, and CDs in their cases). It all will be taken by Bay State Books which supports Literacy projects such as The Prison Book program, Operation Paperback, and many friends of the library groups throughout Massachusetts. But that’s not all! For textiles, bring anything you can wear, sleep in, or dry yourself off with regardless of condition (torn, worn, stained, missing buttons, broken zippers, etc.)! This includes any type of material composed of natural or synthetic fibers, such as products made from wool, silk, linen, cotton, polyester, leather, vinyl, hemp, and rayon. But that’s still not all! In addition, Helpsy takes belts, ties, handkerchiefs, bandanas, wallets, purses, backpacks, totes, footwear, bedding and covers, halloween costumes, curtains, drapes, fabric shades, shower curtains, placemats, tablecloths, throw rugs, fabric mats, and even stuffed animals. The only requirement is that it be clean, dry, and odorless and loaded in bags or boxes. The textiles will be directly loaded in an electric truck run by Helpsy -- a Public Benefit (“B) Corporation whose mission is to keep clothes out of the trash and to create honorable work. In 2025 alone, Hepsy collected over 32 million pounds of clothes, shoes, and other items, 95% of what were reused or recycled.

title: Walk to End Alzheimer's - Greater Boston
description: The Alzheimer's Association invites the community to join the Greater Boston Walk to End Alzheimer's on October 25, 2026, at DCR Richard McKinnon Park in Cambridge. The Walk is the world's largest event dedicated to raising awareness and funds for Alzheimer's care, support, and research. More than 7 million Americans are living with Alzheimer's, and nearly 12 million family members and friends provide unpaid care for loved ones living with the disease. Funds raised through the Walk help the Alzheimer's Association advance critical research efforts while providing free support, education, and resources to families facing Alzheimer's and other dementias. The Greater Boston Walk brings together individuals, families, caregivers, community organizations, and corporate teams who are united in the fight against Alzheimer's and all other dementia. Participants of all ages are welcome and can register as individuals or as part of a team. As part of the event, participants are invited to take part in the Promise Garden ceremony, a moving tribute that honors those impacted by Alzheimer's and other dementias. Each flower in the Promise Garden represents a personal connection to the disease and serves as a powerful symbol of hope and determination. This year, the Walk to End Alzheimer's - Greater Boston is expected to have about 5,000 participants and participants are working together toward a fundraising goal of raising $2 million to support the Alzheimer's Association's mission. Those interested in joining the movement can register, donate, or learn more at act.alz.org/GreaterBoston.

title: October Harvard Square Book Circle
description: Join us for our October Harvard Square Book Circle meeting! This month we’re discussing Ghostland: An American History in Haunted Places by Colin Dickey. Don’t forget each book we discuss is part of our featured Select 70 for frequent buyer members . The Book Circle is Harvard Book Store’s monthly book club open for members of the community to meet and discuss a thoughtfully selected book. We’ll meet in the third room of the store from 6–7:30 PM. Registration is not required and no commitment is necessary. We love new participants! If you are interested in joining the Book Circle’s email list, sign up through this form . About Ghostland One of NPR’s Great Reads of 2016 From the author of The Unidentified , an intellectual feast for fans of offbeat history that takes readers on a road trip through some of the country’s most infamously haunted places—and deep into the dark side of our history. Colin Dickey is on the trail of America’s ghosts. Crammed into old houses and hotels, abandoned prisons and empty hospitals, the spirits that linger continue to capture our collective imagination, but why? His own fascination piqued by a house hunt in Los Angeles that revealed derelict foreclosures and “zombie homes,” Dickey embarks on a journey across the continental United States to decode and unpack the American history repressed in our most famous haunted places. Some have established reputations as “the most haunted mansion in America,” or “the most haunted prison”; others, like the haunted Indian burial grounds in West Virginia, evoke memories from the past our collective nation tries to forget. With boundless curiosity, Dickey conjures the dead by focusing on questions of the living — how do we, the living, deal with stories about ghosts, and how do we inhabit and move through spaces that have been deemed, for whatever reason, haunted? Paying attention not only to the true facts behind a ghost story, but also to the ways in which changes to those facts are made — and why

Majestic Healing Pathways™ is the foundational care model that guides all of Majestic Community Wellness’s programs. It reflects our belief that healing is a right — not a privilege — and that healing happens most sustainably when care is consistent, culturally grounded, and rooted in community. Developed in response to gaps in traditional health and wellness systems, Majestic Healing Pathways™ centers the lived experiences of Black and Brown communities who face disproportionate stress, trauma, and barriers to care. The model honors the reality that healing is not a single intervention, but a pathway built over time through breath, movement, rest, relationship, and choice. The births of her two children inspired her to deepen her studies in prenatal and postnatal yoga. She focused much of her teaching on supporting families and children through the various stages of development. title: Spookey Ruben
description: Spookey Ruben Spookey Ruben @spookeyruben Alice Cohen @alicedesoda Monkey @meammonkey The Freakshadows @hanfreitasmusic + DJ mXe @basicbitch42069 ARTIST BIOS: Spookey Ruben is undoubtedly a household name in the Canadian indie scene, an artist who has stayed unmistakably authentic across three decades. Emerging in the mid-1990s, he has built a body of work defined by playful eccentricity and an intuitive grasp of pop that never sacrifices curiosity in favor of convention. Spookey’s music is a sophisticated combination of childlike wonder, formal experimentation, and melodic discipline, aging into something closer to prophecy than nostalgia. Born Alan Deil in Ottawa, Spookey spent much of his childhood moving through Europe, where his father worked as an engineer for the European Space Agency. A restless adolescence in Germany and the Netherlands gave way to thrash metal, long hair, and the nickname “Spooky”, later stylized as the instantly recognizable “Spookey.” Settling in Washington, D.C. in his high school years, Spookey formed the band Transilience , whose 1990 release Mouthful of Buildings became a cornerstone of avant-garde thrash jazz. He then moved to Toronto at nineteen to study film at York University. There, he drifted back toward music, accumulating ideas on a home four-track that would become the foundation of Spookey Ruben. Those bedroom recordings became Modes of Transportation Vol. 1 , a debut that immediately set him apart from his contemporaries. Crowned “Pet Sounds of the 90s”, the album catapulted him into critical acclaim through its densely imagined world: fairy-tale introductions, yodeling vocals, lullabies that drifted into darkness, and collage-like sound design sitting comfortably alongside impeccably crafted pop hooks. Drawing from the elasticity and moods of 1980s British new wave while filtering those influences through his distinctly personal lens, Spookey established a musical language that felt both referential and entirely his own.

title: Thomas Frank at Harvard Book Store
description: Harvard Book Store welcomes Thomas Frank —a founding editor of The Baffler, a former columnist for The Wall Street Journal, and the bestselling author of What’s the Matter with Kansas? and Listen, Liberal —for a discussion of his new book The Creativity Con: How Innovation Became America’s Biggest Racket. About The Creativity Con A bold indictment of America’s chronic obsession with creativity and innovation, tracing how these beloved ideas came to dominate our political and economic conversation while serving to mask inequality and protect elite interests. “Innovation” and “creativity” have been the defining watchwords of American exceptionalism for decades. They’re deployed by business leaders, tech gurus, military strategists, educators, and urban planners to describe our unique standing in the world. While other countries supposedly suffer from regimentation and a fatal lack of imagination, the United States is often portrayed as an unmatched dynamo of new ideas and products. In The Creativity Con , Thomas Frank disabuses us of this notion, offering a provocative account of the way creativity and innovation have been used as a kind of ideological cover for policies that reinforce the class system. Frank charts the construction of America’s glamorous self-image from Sputnik to Silicon Valley, Apple to Lockheed Martin, Madison Avenue to Main Street, Richard Florida to Donald Trump. He deconstructs the innovation agendas touted by politicians; reads pop psychology; tours SXSW, the mecca of creativity, where musicians mingle with Pentagon officials; and looks in on the cafés, sidewalk murals, and bike lanes that populate the neighborhoods built for the creative class. Along the way, Frank uncovers the insidious effects of centering innovation and creativity in our rhetoric while, in practice, nurturing exactly the opposite. His teaching draws upon his experience in the classroom, rehearsal room, and on the Broadway stage to help dancers integrate technique, musicality, character, and storytelling. About Lethal Kiss A blood-soaked love story of rage, revenge, and belonging, Taylor Grothe’s adult debut is a sapphic horror/romance that’s as grotesque as it is beautiful. Preston University wasn’t Marcella’s first choice of employment, but there’s only so many deaths that can be chalked up to mysterious circumstances before people get suspicious, and her 300 years on Earth have taught her how to pack up and move quickly. She’s resolved to keep her head down and enjoy a couple semesters at Preston—and keep her feedings few and far between. That is, until a professor is found murdered on campus, and it’s not her doing. When Lacie was hired as an assistant professor at Preston a year ago, she knew not everyone makes tenure. But when her only friend disappears without a word, she begins to suspect that her other missing coworkers didn’t just quit. Unfortunately, there’s only one person she can trust enough to ask for help—the beautiful, aloof, and tantalizingly secretive latecomer, Marcella. Lacie and Marcella team up to make a chilling discovery: there’s something festering under the marble floors of Preston University, and it’s hungry. Marcella might be a monster, but the deeper into the mystery they dig, the more she’s attracted to Lacie’s immovable bravery and quiet intelligence. Majestic Healing Pathways™ is the foundational care model that guides all of Majestic Community Wellness’s programs. It reflects our belief that healing is a right — not a privilege — and that healing happens most sustainably when care is consistent, culturally grounded, and rooted in community. Developed in response to gaps in traditional health and wellness systems, Majestic Healing Pathways™ centers the lived experiences of Black and Brown communities who face disproportionate stress, trauma, and barriers to care. The model honors the reality that healing is not a single intervention, but a pathway built over time through breath, movement, rest, relationship, and choice. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? For more than 20 years, Nora has been teaching yoga and dance to students of all ages. The births of her two children inspired her to deepen her studies in prenatal and postnatal yoga. She focused much of her teaching on supporting families and children through the various stages of development. During this time, she earned her Prenatal Yoga Certification through OM Yoga

title: Intermediate/Advanced Ballet with Dean Vollick
description: Class begins with a thorough set of exercises at the barre that last from 30 to 45 minutes. Centre practice follows, and may consist of a battement tendu exercise, a battement jeté exercise, a grand battement exercise, small and/or large adage, stationary turns, traveling turns, and petite and grand allegro enchaînement (small and big jumps). Classes are structured so that the dancer warms up their feet, legs, hips and upper body gradually. As class progresses there are more changes of weight and eventually, sudden changes of direction. Live music is provided by a pianist, that ranges from classical pieces to selections from ballet repertoire to improvisational contemporary music. Cost: $20 Single Class | $15.00 barre | 5-class package $90.00 *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. Please register in studio with the class assistant Accepted Payments: Cash, Check, Venmo What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Ballet originated in the Italian Renaissance courts around 1500 as large balls or spectacles that were performed by members of the royal court. The French king, Louis XIV, created the first academy and the positions, steps, and movements of the ballet were collected and codified. The spectacles began to be performed by artists that were trained in the academy, originally as part of an opera, and later as ballets that told a story through music, mime, and dance. Over the centuries ballet has influenced folk dance styles of many (mainly European) nations and, more recently, has been influenced by folk, modern, and contemporary forms of dance from all countries. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I had a professional dance career that spanned more than twenty years and included company work in both ballet and contemporary companies as well as dancing, choreographing, and teaching as a freelance artist.

description: Join Ally Cirelli, curator of Alfonso Ossorio: Line and Lineage (October 23, 2026–April 11, 2027) at the Harvard Art Museums, and Danni Shen, curator of Knowledge Is Myth: Chimeric Continuities (October 1–December 13, 2026) at the Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts, for a multi-site tour of the two interconnected exhibitions. At the Harvard Art Museums exhibition, we will explore the experimental processes of modern artist Alfonso Ossorio and work by contemporary artists Enzo Camacho and Ami Lien that respond to his artistic legacy in the Philippines. Continuing to the Carpenter Center, we will view more works by Ossorio, Camacho, and Lien as well as other contemporary artists working with mythology. Throughout the tour, Cirelli and Shen will highlight the intergenerational connections made by these artists through material experimentation. Led by: Ally Cirelli, Cunningham Senior Curatorial Assistant for the Collection, Division of Modern and Contemporary Art, Harvard Art Museums Danni Shen, Senior Curatorial and Public Programs Assistant, Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts Alfonso Ossorio: Line and Lineage is made possible through the generous support of the Ossorio Fund, with additional support from the Recharge Foundation Fund for Contemporary Art. , Fund for Modern and Contemporary Art.

title: Beginner NY Salsa
description: Classes will be broken into 5 sections at Level 1. New sessions start the first Monday of every odd month. Warmup Footwork Review Foundational move for Level 1 On2 Linear Salsa (of which there are 7) Dance with Music Philosophically things to be on the lookout for, the importance of melding footwork and partner-work when dancing Salsa, the importance of spaced repetition, the importance of tying everything to Social dancing, and personal convolutional schemes to try to attenuate the lead/follow dichotomy. No partner required. *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. *Students who purchase a membership for the Dance Complex will get that $25 taken off their 10 class new student rate, bringing it down to $85. Cost: $23 Single Class | $85 for 5-Class Package | $130 for 10-Class Package | $110 for new student 10-class package Cash, Venmo (@Brendan-Folan), Zelle (bjfoley21@gmail.com) REGISTRATION: Not Required, Drop-Ins Welcome What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Linear Salsa is a hybrid dance that comes from Mambo (a Cuban style that was popularized in the 1950’s NYC Palladium). NY Mambo is a marriage of footwork and partner-work from Cuba (Aftro-Cuban movements, Cuban Son) and the U.S. (Jazz, Swing). Salsa is a marketing term popularized in the 1970’s to commodify all Latin music and dance to a U.S. audience. Circular Salsa primarily comes from the Cuban dance Casino, which itself originates from Cuban Son. Salsa is by nature transformational, multinational, and multigenerational, embodying the shared heritage of Latin music. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I was the assistant teacher of this class for over 2 years under Ricardo Contreras. I’ve been taking classes from Juan Lopez for over 7 years. I started my Salsa journey learning New York Style Salsa On2 in Worcester. I also work at the Havana Club

title: Live Blues & Roots Music Returns to Harvard Square: Wednesday Nights @ The Sea Hag Restaurant & Bar
description: The Sea Hag Restaurant & Bar and The Barrett Anderson Band are excited to announce a new weekly series, Blues & Roots Wednesdays , bringing live music back home to historic Harvard Square. “Cambridge, our fair city, and I share deep roots, and I’m thrilled to find a new musical home at The Sea Hag,” says Massachusetts-based singer/guitarist, Barrett Anderson. “Good music and good food are two of our most basic, fundamental needs,” he continues, “What great joy they give us. I am so happy to revel in that every Wednesday night with my dearest musical friends, and Kari and her incredible team at The Sea Hag. We go way back together, and I can’t imagine all the fun we have ahead.” Indeed, Anderson has strong connections to this scene. He remembers: “My first professional experience came when I was 15, backing up Muddy Waters’ band alums Pinetop Perkins and Bob Margolin at the original House of Blues on Winthrop Street. A few months after that I began busking, you’d often find me in Brattle Square or by the pit. This would have been mid/late 90s.” While still a teen, Anderson was a member of The Monster Mike Welch Band and Ronnie Earl & The Broadcasters (“Ronnie was my guitar hero. Then he was my teacher, then my boss. Now he’s my musical Father,” Anderson says), before eventually starting The Barrett Anderson Band in 2007. Anderson won a Boston Music Award (2013 Blues Artist of the Year), was on the Billboard charts (2020’s live album Hynoboogie spent 3 weeks on the Billboard Blues Album chart, peaking at #6), and was nominated for a Blues Music Award (2023 Band of the Year with Anthony Geraci & The Boston Blues All-Stars), all the while playing nationally, internationally, and locally in Cambridge and the greater Boston area. In addition to the musical roots, long-time locals may recognize Anderson from a decade serving tables and bartending at The Sea Hag’s sister establishment, Grendel’s Den, or from Abodeon, the mid-century modern shop started by his family. title: Wendy S. Walters at Harvard Book Store
description: Harvard Book Store welcomes Wendy S. Walters —associate professor of nonfiction in the Writing Program of the School of the Arts at Columbia University and author of Multiply/Divide: On the American Real and Surreal —for a discussion of her new book, A Dead White: An Argument Against White Paint. About A Dead White An impassioned, boundary-pushing work of criticism traversing an array of subjects, from fine arts to design to architecture, taking aim at the ubiquity of white paint in our society and what its prevalence reveals about our values. It’s hard to identify a material that takes up more sensory space and has received less critical examination than white paint. As the default color of our built environment, it asks us to believe that it’s neutral—that it has no signifiers or, perhaps more troublingly, that what it does signify, whether it be calmness, cleanliness, blankness, or purity, is unassailable and value-free. In this expansive, impassioned examination, cultural critic Wendy S. Walters interrogates all that we have taken for granted about the substance that colors, or fails to color, the structures and objects that surround us—and what the collective impulse toward white paint can tell us about culture, politics, and individual desire. Tracing the unquantifiable impact of white paint on our lived environment and in our collective imaginary, A Dead White braids together multiple narrative threads and associations. Exploring the role of white paint in art history, architecture, and consumer culture, it follows its influence into the home, the halls of the workplace, the galleries and studios of the contemporary art world, and larger forums of mass culture and national identity, never losing sight of how this cultural inclination manifests in our choices and habits as individuals. title: Hunter Flynn: Back to My Roots Tour
description: Hunter Flynn: Back to My Roots Tour With special guest Evan Cyote Presented by The Rockwell and Peachtree Entertainment. Hunter Flynn is a Kentucky-born singer-songwriter and visual artist whose work resonates with emotional honesty and a deep connection to Appalachian culture. Raised in Pulaski County, Flynn’s path to music and art wasn’t a straight line—it was forged through adversity and personal transformation. In early 2022, after surviving a life-altering car accident, he decided to fully embrace his creative passions, launching a music career rooted in authenticity, vulnerability, and soul. Drawing inspiration from the landscapes and stories of Appalachia, Flynn blends elements of folk, country, soul, and gospel into a genre-defying sound he calls Appalachian Soul Music. His lyrics, often reflective and raw, tell stories of pain, redemption, resilience, and identity—underscored by his powerful vocals and minimalist arrangements. These qualities are showcased in his debut EP, Appalachian Soul, released in May 2023, which quickly gained traction for its emotional depth and stripped-back sincerity. Learn more about Hunter Flynn and his music at www.hunterflynn.com . title: A Closer Look at Charley Longfellow’s “Japan Room"
description: Charles Appleton Longfellow (1844–1893), the eldest son of poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow and Frances Appleton Longfellow, was a globetrotter and avid collector. During his 20-month stay in Japan (1871–1873), he purchased and shipped home to Cambridge dozens of crates of artworks and decorative objects for himself, friends, and family. Upon his return in 1874, Charley transformed the sitting room at his family home into a “Japan Room” with the help of his cousin Alexander Wadsworth Longfellow (1854–1934). One of its most striking features was a ceiling decorated with more than 35 fan-shaped paintings arranged in a “scattered fan” pattern. Although Japanese art and decorative objects had entered U.S. markets by the mid-1870s, their availability and visibility varied considerably by city. Created in 1874, on the eve of the transformative 1876 Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia, the Japan Room represents an unusually early American domestic interior devoted to Japanese art and design. This lecture examines its remarkable ceiling of fan paintings, exploring their origins and arrangement and considering how this distinctive feature of the room reflects the ways Japanese art was displayed and experienced in nineteenth-century America. This research was supported by the Friends of the Longfellow House-Washington's Headquarters 2025 Art Research Fellowship Program. ————————————— Elizabeth K. Eder, Ph.D., is a museum scholar, educator, and researcher who has worked at the Smithsonian Institution for more than 20 years, including at the Smithsonian American Art Museum, the National Museum of Asian Art (formerly the Freer Gallery of Art and Arthur M. Sackler Gallery), and the Anacostia Community Museum. Her museum career has also included positions at the Walters Art Museum, the National Gallery of Art, and the American Alliance of Museums. Working across painting, murals, and sculpture, she uses calligraphic repetition to create meditative spaces of color and gesture that foster reflection, protection, and pride. Speakers: Sneha Shrestha, Artist Sarah Laursen, Alan J. title: CPL Presents America Unfinished: 250 Years of Law and Governance (Main)
description: Join editors Alexandra Natapoff and Guy-Uriel Charles, along with contributors to America Unfinished: 250 Years of Law and Governance, for a discussion of this new collection of essays marking America’s 250th anniversary. America Unfinished brings together more than 50 legal scholars from the Harvard Law School faculty to examine a pivotal moment in American law and governance. The collection’s 62 essays explore topics including the expansion of executive power, the relationship between workers, consumers, and markets, democratic accountability in a market-driven economy, and the future of knowledge and governance institutions amid rapid technological change. Contributors include Stephen Breyer, Tomiko Brown-Nagin, Noah Feldman, Annette Gordon-Reed, Randall Kennedy, Jill Lepore, Lawrence Lessig, Bruce H. Mann, Martha Minow, and Cass R. Sunstein. description: In this class, you’ll explore earthy Egyptian, Turkish, and American style movements, dynamic combinations, and expressive choreography blending tradition and innovation. Experience the power of fiery hip-locks and shimmies, and the fluid beauty of serpentine undulations. Drawing from decades of study with master teachers and over thirty years of performance experience, Johara offers expert guidance in a supportive, inspiring environment—honoring the depth of this ancient art while inviting each student to discover their own unique style within it. Instructions: Wear comfortable dance or workout clothing that allows you to move freely. Classes are danced barefoot or in dance shoes. The more authentic name for this dance form is raqs sharqi (“dance of the East”), and its roots lie in the Middle and Near East, primarily in Egypt and Turkey. This dance form was introduced to the United States and Europe at the turn of the 20th century, but it was not widely performed or taught until the 1950s and 1960s, when the belly dance craze swept across the U.S. The American cabaret style of belly dance is rooted in the legacy passed down by notable American teachers and performers, who blended Middle Eastern influences with their own innovations and movement styles drawn from diverse dance backgrounds. title: Dr. Raj Panjabi at Harvard Book Store
description: Harvard Book Store welcomes Dr. Raj Panjabi —Former White House Senior Director, Senior Partner at Flagship Pioneering, and Associate Physician at Mass General Brigham and Harvard Medical School—for a discussion of his new book, Safer: A Playbook—Turning Fear into Action and Crisis into Community. About Safer The essential guide for navigating crisis and uncertainty from the acclaimed physician who led the White House response to the world’s most dangerous health emergencies. When crisis hits—a sudden illness, a global disruption, or a career upheaval—our instinct is to retreat. Yet decades of research prove that our greatest protection isn’t isolation, it’s connection. From high-stakes decisions in the White House Situation Room and hospital emergency room to dramatic shocks of violence and illness his family struggled with in their own living room, Dr. Raj Panjabi has navigated humanity’s most precarious moments. Now, he translates hard-earned wisdom into a step-by-step roadmap. Through gripping storytelling and cutting-edge science, Safer reveals the eight practical “plays” to protect what matters most at home and work. You will learn how to: Navigate Fear and Denial: Use Situation Room insights to take decisive action without falling into paralysis. Cut Through the Noise: Use science to assess your risk and protect those you love amidst the flood of misinformation. Build Trust in Divided Times: Move from isolation to connection and find common ground. Gain Control Despite Chaos: Adapt to change and transform vulnerability into your greatest strength. In an era of uncertainty, you don’t have to live in fear. You just need a better playbook. Safer gives us the tools for emerging from any crisis more connected than ever before.

title: Gillian Margot & Geoffrey Keezer
description: Regattabar is proud to welcome acclaimed vocalist Gillian Margot and piano virtuoso Geoffrey Keezer! This magical duo present an intimate musical conversation that spans the breadth of the American Songbook and beyond, with masterful interpretations that showcase their remarkable artistic chemistry. Blending technical brilliance with emotional depth, Margot and Keezer—partners in music and life for over a decade —create a performance environment of boundless flexibility and mutual responsiveness, allowing each song to unfold with spontaneity while honoring the rich traditions from which they draw inspiration. Don’t miss these two world-class artists in concert together! “Within the first few seconds of the first song from Gillian Margot and Geoffrey Keezer, …I had the glorious sense of having had my expectations fulfilled, the feeling that everything that would happen thereafter – and there was a lot – would come as a bonus.” — Sebastian Scotney, UK Jazz News “[Keezer} is a brilliant soloist and a sensitive accompanist. Paired with the sincere and masterful vocalist, Gillian Margot, they make an outstanding duo.” — Dee Dee McNeil, Making a Scene “Give the couple ten pieces of magic to work on and the resulting product is beyond perfection.” — Lance Liddle, Bebop Spoken Here “Margot’s got one of those voices you don’t forget — rich, smoky, and totally in control, gliding across registers with ease. description: This class reviews cross-body lead and covers inside turn, half right turn, and cumbia turns, combining them with basic right and left turns. Cost: $20 Single Class | $90 for 5-Class Package *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. Salsa is a musical and dance style that originated in Cuba with African roots and European influences. It later developed in New York and it’s popular throughout Latin America in places like Puerto Rico, Colombia, Peru and Cuba just to name a few. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I grew up listening to Salsa music and later got interested in the dance. Salsa dancing is a social dance that help break barriers and brings people together from all walks of life. It also gives you the opportunity to express yourself freely on the dance floor or stage. title: Changing the Rules: Designers Who Shape What Gets Built | Seattle, WA
description: Join GSD community members in Seattle, WA, for the second installment of theGSD Alumni Lecture Series. Sponsored by theGSD Alumni Counciland theHarvard Club of Seattle, this panel brings together four GSD alumni who have changed the rules governing what gets built through model-building codes, municipal administration, policy analysis, and elected office. These distinguished practitioners will discuss what prompted them to move beyond individual projects, what this change cost them in time and career momentum, and how others can get involved. Q&A to follow. Refreshments will be served. Special thanks toDarren Chang (MArch ’08)of Darren Vinci Architecture & Design for organizing and toMelissa Alexander (MAUD ’13), Data Visualization Principal at Blue Cottage of CannonDesign, for moderating. Questions? ContactDevelopment & Alumni Relations. Susan Jones (MArch ’88) is the founder of atelierjones LLC. atelierjones has been a national leader in designing and building early mass timber buildings in the US since 2012. She represented AIA National on the ICC Tall Wood Building Committee to adopt the tall mass timber code in the 2021-2024 code cycles. In 2025, atelierjones represented the US in the Venice Biennale. Peter Steinbrueck (LF ’10) is principal of Steinbrueck Urban Strategies. Peter helped lead the Citizens Alternative Plan initiative before holding office, serving ten years on the Seattle City Council, including a term as president and four years chairing urban development and planning. Lisa Rutzick (MUP ’98) is a Customer Experience Product Manager bringing human-centered design and user research methods to support permitting and technology at the City of Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections. Prior to this role, Lisa worked in Land Use and then managed Seattle’s Design Review program for many years. Radhika Nair (MUP ’07) is the founder of Seva Workshop. title: A Fresh New Scene in Navarra
description: Saturday, October 24, 6:30-8pm ET Young winemakers are marrying local pride with international experience to make world-class wines. With its northerly spot (between Rioja and France) and cool Atlantic breezes, Navarra is turning out lively wines brimming with freshness and acidity. Ranging from richly-hued rosés to almost black old-vines specimens, the wines offer freshness and complexity, whether made with just garnacha , or blended with other grapes such as tempranillo, cabernet sauvignon, or syrah . title: MAIN STAGE: Anthony Leva | Faculty Debut Recital
description: Music made to heal people, played by a string band that improvises its way there. Gnawa musicians in Morocco play through the night to move a room from one state into another. Ornette Coleman, Don Cherry, and Henry Grimes chased something similar through free jazz. Tony Leva puts both lineages in the same room for his Longy faculty debut. A modern string band, original compositions, and long stretches of free improvisation. Expect the evening to end somewhere nobody planned. Longy’s performance are free and open to the public, but please register in advance.

title: Edward Steed at Harvard Book Store
description: Harvard Book Store welcomes Edward Steed —award-winning cartoonist for the New Yorker and Grammy-winner for Best Recording Package for his Father John Misty album cover — for a discussion of his new book, Happy Hour: A Book of Drawings. He will be joined in conversation with Ruth Lichtman — Emmy-nominated director and producer of film, audio, and theatre. About Happy Hour A generational talent’s old cartooning soul returns for a second round. Edward Steed continues his winning streak as the most exciting cartoonist in The New Yorker’s pages in the 21st century. Hailed as the last great hope of the single panel gag strip, the sole saving grace of a print media taking its last dying breaths, Steed brings a deftly scrawled lacerating sense of humour that alludes to classic New Yorker cartoonists like Charles Addams, William Steig, and Sol Stenberg as well as modern cringe alt-comedy. With Happy Hour out hot on the heels of his best-selling and critically-lauded debut collection, Forces of Nature , Steed proves he’s no flash in the pan but an enduring comedic talent. Every page in this collection is a hilarious master class on how to tickle a funnybone.

description: In this 90-minute workshop, you’ll learn the basics of sewing machine operation and safety. description: Entrance to the historic house is by guided tour only, and all tours are free of charge. What does this house reveal about our shared past? Here, history was made, and history was written. Highlighting the house and its remarkable collections (original to the Longfellow period), this conversational tour will explore links between colonial-era slavery and freedom, Washington’s headquarters at the start of the American Revolution, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s poetic legacy, and the Longfellow family’s legacy of historic preservation.

title: Stems & Sips: Sake & Ikebana
description: Saturday, October 31, 6:30-8:00pm EST Find your flow, one branch and one pour at a time. True harmony happens when you strip things down to their absolute essence. In Japan, this philosophy connects two beautiful crafts: Ikebana (minimalist floral arrangement) and Sake (the refined art of brewing). Join us for Stems & Sips, a relaxed, hands-on evening designed for beginners. No complex jargon, no overwhelming flower bundles—just clean flavors, striking lines, and a healthy dose of fun. What to Expect Sake Demystified: Discover the stunning versatility of premium sake. You’ll taste a curated flight—ranging from bright and fruity to crisp and earthy—while learning the basics of how it’s made and served. The Living Sculpture: Dive into Ikebana, the traditional art of flower arrangement. Unlike dense Western bouquets, Ikebana focuses on negative space, asymmetry, and making a few thoughtful stems speak volumes. Guided Creation: We will walk you through the core principles of line, depth, and form. Step-by-step, you’ll learn how to position branches and blossoms to mimic the grace of nature. No experience required. We provide the tools, the knowledge, and the liquid inspiration. You’ll leave with a gorgeous centerpiece, a newfound appreciation for Japanese craft, and a serious sense of zen. title: The Commute
description: The Commute SHOW DESCRIPTION: Four strangers are trapped in a tunnel during a sudden stop on the Red Line. As tension builds, they are forced to confront each other-and themselves. The Commute is a dark, thought provoking new comedy by Karin Anell, exploring human behavior under pressure. Who are we really, behind our masks? The evening show will be followed by an interactive talk-back and panel discussing the evolving role of technology in our lives. ARTIST STATEMENT: “I love listening to people’s life stories. My scripts are often based on individuals’ lived experiences and I believe in theatre as a powerful vehicle to bring these engaging narratives to life. Theatre can bring people together to start important conversations, and I don’t mean discussions around who was the better actor, or whether the third act was too long. I want people to leave the theatre and spend the next couple of hours discussing what they saw. How did this piece make them feel? What are they thinking right now? Did this play open their eyes to something new; see the world, and themselves, in a different light? I like to include interactive sessions with a subject matter expert(s) after performances. I moderate these sessions, inviting the audience to participate and ask questions about what they saw. Themes I have brought to life include a mother’s guilt, body image, and our biggest fears. It does not take a million-dollar production that runs for 3 hours to engage an audience and stimulate an interesting debate. I believe in: Simplicity and adaptability-use modern technology to make theatre more engaging and entertaining Short plays that pack a punch, using local talent Community-based theatre accessible to all” — Karin Anell SOCIAL MEDIAS: Facebook: tcsquaredthea tre / Instagram: @tc2theatre Timeline: EARLY SHOW: DOORS: 1:15 PM SHOW: 2:00 PM LATE SHOW (With Panel!): DOORS: 5:15 PM SHOW: 6:00 PM Age Limit: Some mature themes. title: Multispecies Warfare in Palestine-Israel: A talk by Irus Braverman
description: Brook Farm Institute for Critical Studies welcomes Radcliffe scholar Irus Braverman as the next speaker in our ongoing public lecture series, Critical Interventions. Animals have long played important roles in human warfare. Drawing on ethnographic research and on her own experiences growing up in Palestine-Israel, Braverman will explore how nonhuman animals have become active participants in Israeli warfare and how warfare itself has been shaped by their presence. Introducing the concept of “multispecies warfare,” she will show that animals are not simply instruments of military violence, but that they also acquire political significance through animal welfare regulations, animal rights initiatives, property regimes, and environmental protections. Sheep seize territory through grazing, dogs become subjects of rescue and humanization, donkeys sustain mobility under siege, crocodiles operate as imagined security technologies, and camel movement becomes criminalized through conservation laws. Warfare, then, is enacted through both violence and care. By tracing unexpected connections between humans, animals, and war, Braverman will offer a new way of thinking about warfare itself: not as an exclusively human endeavor, but as a complex multispecies project that shapes political worlds.

title: Inheritance: A Litany
description: “Inheritance: A Litany” is a deeply intimate, yet universal, personal narrative, dance-opera-play, and comic drama created and performed by Janis Brenner. Inspired by Ms. Brenner’s late parents, the 51-minute work is a journey into the myriad of ways Ms. Brenner “became” her parents—inheriting her father’s wavy hair and sarcasm, her mother’s singing voice and fragile bones. The autobiographical one-woman show reveals aspects of a family’s story, as well as the nature of how we become who we are. The interdisciplinary tour-de-force also uncovers what make us each unique, complicated, and fragile human beings. This show is appropriate for ages 14 and up. “We need artists like Ms. Brenner now in this world, as she crosses genres, asks hard questions, and brings a gentleness and tenderness to her rendering of parents who were equal parts loving and exasperating, protecting and needy, known and misunderstood. We emerge emboldened, ready to create our own litanies, ready for family voices to speak.” – Cynthia Darling, All About Solo, 2019 JANIS BRENNER: Janis Brenner is a renowned, multi-award-winning dancer/choreographer/singer/teacher, and Artistic Director of Janis Brenner & Dancers in NYC. Honors include: “Bessie” Award in Meredith Monk’s “The Politics of Quiet”, Lester Horton Award in L.A., Fund for US Artists at International Festivals, U.S. State Department, Asian Cultural Council, The Trust for Mutual Understanding, US Embassies in Moscow, Bosnia, Jakarta and Dakar, O’Donnell Green Music and Dance Foundation (multiple grants) and a commission from the Whitney Museum of American Art for “The Memory Project.” Her work has been commissioned/re-staged on more than 55 companies and colleges worldwide. Brenner worked closely for years with Meredith Monk & Vocal Ensemble, Michael Moschen, Annabelle Gamson, and with Murray Louis Dance Company, Bat Sheva Dance Company and Alwin Nikolais. title: Monday Moments for Friends, Fellows, and Partners
description: We invite Friends, Fellows, and Partners of the museums to explore two fascinating exhibitions at their own pace through a self-guided visit: On Location: Drawing the Outdoors (September 18, 2026–January 17, 2027) and The Way We Never Were: The American Professional Photographers Collection (August 29, 2026–May 9, 2027). In the exhibition On Location: Drawing the Outdoors, discover how an intimate relationship with nature shaped the artistic vision of 19th-century European artists. Featuring approximately 140 sketches, watercolors, and pastels by artists including J. M. W. Turner, Berthe Morisot, Paul Cézanne, and Vincent van Gogh, the exhibition is organized as a series of thematic journeys through the landscape and explores changing ideas about nature, environmental awareness, and artistic identity. It invites visitors to reflect on why these artists’ experiences of the outdoors continue to resonate today. The Way We Never Were explores how professional photography helped shape Americans’ understanding of life after World War II. Drawn from the Harvard Art Museums’ American Professional Photographers Collection, the exhibition features commissioned photographs of weddings, schools, businesses, and other everyday moments that presented an idealized vision of postwar America. These images not only documented the era but also influenced cultural memory by highlighting certain experiences while leaving others out. Through themes of prosperity, suburbia, conformity, and the struggle for equal rights, the exhibition encourages visitors to reconsider the story these photographs tell about the American past. This special preview is our way of thanking you for your support and dedication to the Harvard Art Museums. To become a Friend, Fellow, or Partner, please visit our Support page. Join today to take advantage of this exclusive opportunity. Funding for On Location: Drawing the Outdoors and related programming was provided by the Stanley H. Durwood Foundation Support Fun

title: Rachel Dorothy Tanur Memorial Lecture: Pneuhaus “Building with Air”
description: Pneuhaus began by blowing bubbles: a joint thesis project built around a fascination with inflatables and what could be made of them at a craft level. This talk traces how that early curiosity grew into a full-fledged art, design, and fabrication studio. Working hands-on with materials and techniques eventually shaped an unusual business model, closer to a traveling circus than a design studio, where work packs down small, travels light, and can go up almost anywhere in the world. August Lehrecke, Pneuhaus co-founder, will cover how making and installing their work built the studio Pneuhaus runs today, and how commissioned projects sharpen the skills and tools they carry back into the creative practice. Underneath it all is a fascination with how much a shift in air pressure can change: soft turns rigid, a surface lets light through or blocks it out, or a structure deforms underfoot. Lehrecke will discuss various studio projects and the areas the studio is currently exploring.

title: Deni Elliott at Harvard Book Store
description: Harvard Book Store welcomes Deni Elliott —co-director for the National Ethics Project and professor emerita in the Department of Journalism and Digital Communication at the University of South Florida—for a discussion of her new book, Catching Sight: How a Guide Dog Helped Me See Myself. About Catching Sight One woman’s journey through progressive blindness and the extraordinary guide dog who kept her safe along the way. When ethics scholar Deni Elliott, born with limited vision, realized she could no longer navigate the world safely alone, she turned to a guide dog—a decision that reshaped her understanding of disability and independence. Written in collaboration with master trainer Graham Buck, Catching Sight offers a behind-the-scenes look at the world of guide dog breeding and training, revealing the intelligence and decision-making skills these dogs develop from birth. Catching Sight is for readers interested in the transformative power of human relationships with animals. As Deni confronts her changing reality, she shares the hidden world of guide dog training and introduces Alberta, a yellow Lab whose quiet brilliance changed her interaction with the world and herself. Catching Sight offers a fresh and unforgettable perspective on disability, identity, and the power of partnership.

Linear Salsa is a hybrid dance that comes from Mambo (a Cuban style that was popularized in the 1950’s NYC Palladium). Majestic Healing Pathways™ is the foundational care model that guides all of Majestic Community Wellness’s programs. It reflects our belief that healing is a right — not a privilege — and that healing happens most sustainably when care is consistent, culturally grounded, and rooted in community. Developed in response to gaps in traditional health and wellness systems, Majestic Healing Pathways™ centers the lived experiences of Black and Brown communities who face disproportionate stress, trauma, and barriers to care. The model honors the reality that healing is not a single intervention, but a pathway built over time through breath, movement, rest, relationship, and choice. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? For more than 20 years, Nora has been teaching yoga and dance to students of all ages. She completed her 200-hour teacher training at Atmananda Yoga, and her teaching continues to be informed by years of study in Pilates, Feldenkrais, Hot Yoga, and Katonah Yoga. description: Class begins with a thorough set of exercises at the barre that last from 30 to 45 minutes. Centre practice follows, and may consist of a battement tendu exercise, a battement jeté exercise, a grand battement exercise, small and/or large adage, stationary turns, traveling turns, and petite and grand allegro enchaînement (small and big jumps). Classes are structured so that the dancer warms up their feet, legs, hips and upper body gradually. As class progresses there are more changes of weight and eventually, sudden changes of direction. Ballet originated in the Italian Renaissance courts around 1500 as large balls or spectacles that were performed by members of the royal court. The French king, Louis XIV, created the first academy and the positions, steps, and movements of the ballet were collected and codified. The spectacles began to be performed by artists that were trained in the academy, originally as part of an opera, and later as ballets that told a story through music, mime, and dance. Over the centuries ballet has influenced folk dance styles of many (mainly European) nations and, more recently, has been influenced by folk, modern, and contemporary forms of dance from all countries. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I had a professional dance career that spanned more than twenty years and included company work in both ballet and contemporary companies as well as dancing, choreographing, and teaching as a freelance artist.

title: Artist Talk: Enzo Camacho and Ami Lien
description: The 2026 Nancy Stephenson Nichols Memorial Lecture Join visual artists and Harvard alumni Enzo Camacho (A.B. ’07) and Ami Lien (A.B. ’09) as they share insights and developments into their practice as artistic collaborators. Working between New York, Berlin, and Manila, Camacho and Lien develop research-based, site-specific, and documentary projects to examine histories of labor, land, and resistance in the Philippines. Their research on the enduring influence of Alfonso Ossorio’s mural commission at the Chapel of St. Joseph the Worker on Negros Island has led them to investigate the sugar plantation landscape that grounds this historic site-specific artwork. In their ongoing engagement with Negros Island, the artists focus on the defiant forms of culture-making that emerge out of and in opposition to plantation violence. This program is offered in conjunction with Alfonso Ossorio: Line and Lineage (October 23, 2026–April 11, 2027) in Gallery 1120 at the Harvard Art Museums and Knowledge Is Myth: Chimeric Continuities (October 1–December 13, 2026) at the Carpenter Center for Visual Arts. This event is part of In Conversation, a series of evening programs that feature local and international curators, artists, scholars, and more. Running from September through April, these events highlight our temporary exhibitions, permanent collections, and a range of creative voices.

Linear Salsa is a hybrid dance that comes from Mambo (a Cuban style that was popularized in the 1950’s NYC Palladium). NY Mambo is a marriage of footwork and partner-work from Cuba (Aftro-Cuban movements, Cuban Son) and the U.S. (Jazz, Swing). Salsa is a marketing term popularized in the 1970’s to commodify all Latin music and dance to a U.S. audience. Circular Salsa primarily comes from the Cuban dance Casino, which itself originates from Cuban Son. Salsa is by nature transformational, multinational, and multigenerational, embodying the shared heritage of Latin music. title: Live Blues & Roots Music Returns to Harvard Square: Wednesday Nights @ The Sea Hag Restaurant & Bar
description: The Sea Hag Restaurant & Bar and The Barrett Anderson Band are excited to announce a new weekly series, Blues & Roots Wednesdays , bringing live music back home to historic Harvard Square. “Cambridge, our fair city, and I share deep roots, and I’m thrilled to find a new musical home at The Sea Hag,” says Massachusetts-based singer/guitarist, Barrett Anderson. “Good music and good food are two of our most basic, fundamental needs,” he continues, “What great joy they give us. I am so happy to revel in that every Wednesday night with my dearest musical friends, and Kari and her incredible team at The Sea Hag. We go way back together, and I can’t imagine all the fun we have ahead.” Indeed, Anderson has strong connections to this scene. He remembers: “My first professional experience came when I was 15, backing up Muddy Waters’ band alums Pinetop Perkins and Bob Margolin at the original House of Blues on Winthrop Street. A few months after that I began busking, you’d often find me in Brattle Square or by the pit. This would have been mid/late 90s.” While still a teen, Anderson was a member of The Monster Mike Welch Band and Ronnie Earl & The Broadcasters (“Ronnie was my guitar hero. Then he was my teacher, then my boss. Now he’s my musical Father,” Anderson says), before eventually starting The Barrett Anderson Band in 2007. Anderson won a Boston Music Award (2013 Blues Artist of the Year), was on the Billboard charts (2020’s live album Hynoboogie spent 3 weeks on the Billboard Blues Album chart, peaking at #6), and was nominated for a Blues Music Award (2023 Band of the Year with Anthony Geraci & The Boston Blues All-Stars), all the while playing nationally, internationally, and locally in Cambridge and the greater Boston area. In addition to the musical roots, long-time locals may recognize Anderson from a decade serving tables and bartending at The Sea Hag’s sister establishment, Grendel’s Den, or from Abodeon, the mid-century modern shop started by his family. title: Persia to Iran: History, Politics and Visual Culture of a Civilization in the Headlines
description: How much do our students know about Persia/Iran? This program begins in the ancient period with Achaemenid Persia (550–330 B.C.E.), examining Persian ingenuity, political culture and history as we understand it through the historical and archaeological record. The second part of the program jumps forward in time to 20th- and 21st-century Iran, using the Harvard Peabody Museum’s “From Iran: A Visual Testimony” photographic exhibition as an entry point to more recent historical events and Iranian perspectives on them. We will then delve into Iran’s political history and international relations from the early 20th century forward, noting historical continuities with the past as well as ruptures. Bring your questions and curiosity, regardless of the grade level you teach — this will be a remarkable opportunity to engage with expert historians and curators! This program is in collaboration with the Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology at Harvard.

description: In this class, you’ll explore earthy Egyptian, Turkish, and American style movements, dynamic combinations, and expressive choreography blending tradition and innovation. Experience the power of fiery hip-locks and shimmies, and the fluid beauty of serpentine undulations. Drawing from decades of study with master teachers and over thirty years of performance experience, Johara offers expert guidance in a supportive, inspiring environment—honoring the depth of this ancient art while inviting each student to discover their own unique style within it. Instructions: Wear comfortable dance or workout clothing that allows you to move freely. Classes are danced barefoot or in dance shoes. The more authentic name for this dance form is raqs sharqi (“dance of the East”), and its roots lie in the Middle and Near East, primarily in Egypt and Turkey. This dance form was introduced to the United States and Europe at the turn of the 20th century, but it was not widely performed or taught until the 1950s and 1960s, when the belly dance craze swept across the U.S. The American cabaret style of belly dance is rooted in the legacy passed down by notable American teachers and performers, who blended Middle Eastern influences with their own innovations and movement styles drawn from diverse dance backgrounds. The lecture follows a string of recent recognitions for the office, including the 2025 Brussels Architecture Award for Major Intervention, several nominations for the EU Mies Award, and a finalist placement, with Pierre-Antoine Gatier, in the ongoing competition to transform the Opéra Bastille in Paris. title: Jackie Evans – SOLD OUT!
description: Jackie Evans – SOLD OUT! With Elli Rowe For New York-based singer/songwriter Jackie Evans, music has always been the only option, but Evans only began releasing songs under her own name last year. Her style, often likened to the timeless writing of Carole King, Billy Joel, and Sara Bareilles is, in part, the byproduct of years spent taking requests at piano bars. As a gigging musician, Evans has tried it all; from playing standards on cruise ships, to performing at theme parks and majoring in theater. title: Joe Alterman Trio
description: Atlanta native Joe Alterman expresses a certain upbeat naivete, with a broad smile and bright eyes that make you feel welcome. One would not guess that this is a man hailed by greats; Ramsey Lewis describes his music as “happy music with tasty meat on the bones,” Les McCann states “Joe’s on a ‘blow your mind’ level,” and Ahmad Jamal calls him “a very special artist.” Journalist Nat Hentoff championed three of Alterman’s albums, as well as his writing (Joe wrote liner notes to three Wynton Marsalis/JLCO albums), calling one of Joe’s columns “one of the very best pieces on the essence of jazz, the spirit of jazz, that I’ve ever read, and I’m not exaggerating.” Joe Alterman began at NYU with a BA and Masters in Jazz Piano from NYU and has since performed at many world-renowned venues including the Kennedy Center, Lincoln Center, Birdland and Blue Note alongside Houston Person, Les McCann, Dick Gregory, Ramsey Lewis, and his own trio, among others. Downbeat describes his sound as “rooted in the blues, and with a touch reminiscent of the great pianists of the 1950s—Red Garland, Ahmad Jamal, Bill Evans.” It is clear Joe hits all of the necessary points for Jazz critics and fans alike.

title: Materials Lab Workshop: Making an Impression
description: Join assistant paper conservator Abby Schleicher and research curator Francesca Bewer for a workshop focused on art and science. You’ll discover how different printmaking techniques record both intentional design and the physical traces of making. Through hands-on experimentation using a variety of tools, pressures, inks, and papers, you’ll see how each technical choice leaves distinct traces—and why no two impressions are ever truly identical. We’ll look at a selection of prints under magnification and specialized conservation lighting to “read” their toolmarks, plate wear, inking, and condition. Linking studio experiments with close looking from a conservation perspective, this workshop will give you a concrete framework for identifying print processes and a richer appreciation of the material complexity of printed images. This workshop is one of four offered this fall that explore different media through the lens of art and science. Take one or take them all! The four workshops are: Saturday, September 19: Landscape Drawing with Optical Devices Wednesday, October 7: Color Alchemy—Pigments and DIY Paint Friday, November 6: Making an Impression Friday, November 20: Casting Connections—Molds, Replicas, and Questions of Authorship

description: Just back from a second appearance at Lincoln Center, The Perugia Jazz Festival and a European tour with Black Earth Sway, The Zahili Zamora Afro-Cuban Jazz Quartet led by Afro-Cuban jazz pianist and vocalist Zahili Zamora, bassist Gerson Lazo Quiroga, drummer Zack O’Farrill and Special Guest, saxophonist Yosvany Terry checks in at The Regattabar. About Tyrant Lizard Queen From the author of the beloved The Last Days of the Dinosaurs , an imaginative celebration of T. Rex from hatching to adulthood. Tyrannosaurus rex is a prehistoric celebrity. Exceeding 40 feet in length and weighing over 9 tons, the largest individuals of this dinosaurian species were intimidating predators capable of crushing bone and consuming more than a hundred pounds of flesh in a bite. But the last of the tyrant dinosaurs had a life beyond ripping and tearing. More than 66 million years ago, T. rex courted each other, nested, watched over their offspring, slept, drank, and explored ancient floodplains inhabited by a fantastic cast of impressive dinosaurs like the huge long-neck Alamosaurus and burly, three-horned Torosaurus . For the first time, the life story of this impressive, sensitive predator is told as if you were there to watch it unfold. In her latest prehistoric nature walk, bestselling and award-winning author Riley Black follows the life of plucky T. rex Snaggletooth from the time she hatches through her tumultuous adulthood. The prehistoric forest Snag emerges into is full of danger, and yet, as Riley weaves the latest fossil discoveries into the story, the carnivorous dinosaur survives to play, court, fight, sleep, nest, and more as she grows up in Cretaceous North America. She tussles with rival tyrannosaurs, hunts for delectable prey, and finds soft moments of connection in the forest. Even the most die-hard dinosaur fan will come away with a new perspective and appreciation for the Tyrant Lizard Queen.

title: The Art & Science of Feathers
description: In-Person Workshop Location: The Harvard Museum of Natural History, Classroom B (Third Floor), Cambridge, MA 02138 Instructor: Erica Beade and Lorna Gibson Price: $50 members / $60 nonmembers Feathers give birds their color, from the bright red of a male Cardinal to the iridescent reds and greens of Ruby-throated Hummingbirds. Feathers keep birds warm and dry: down provides excellent insulation against heat loss, and water really does roll off a duck’s back. Feathers form the aerodynamic shape of the wing, enabling flight. A Barn Owl’s flight feathers suppress sound, allowing it to fly nearly silently, while its ruff feathers reflect and focus sound into its ears, enabling the owl to hunt in total darkness by sound alone. In this workshop, we’ll look closely at feathers through the eyes of an artist and an engineer. We’ll examine the structure of different types of feathers, see what gives feathers their color, and learn how an owl’s facial ruff feathers enable it to hunt by hearing alone. We’ll alternate between learning about feathers and exploring techniques for capturing them in pencil. All skill levels are welcome. This class is for adults. Maximum class size is 12 attendees.
